title: 1776 at the Walnut Street Theatre
text:
Living in the Philadelphia area, just a 10 min train ride away, is particularly special with all the festivities of the 250th Anniversary of the nation!  I will be posting about some things as I experience them.

Just saw the musical 1776 at The Walnut Street Theatre, founded in 1808, is America's oldest theatre — and also the Official State Theatre of Pennsylvania and a National Historic Landmark. 

Walnut Street Theatre

It's considered not only the oldest theatre in the United States, but also the oldest continuously operating theatre in the entire English-speaking world. (Guinness World Records)
A few fun facts about the building itself: it was the first theatre to install gas footlights (in 1837), the first to feature air conditioning (in 1855), and switched to electric chandeliers and footlights in 1892. 
It originally opened as "The New Circus" before being renamed The Olympic in 1812 and finally became Walnut Street Theatre in 1820. Notably, Edwin Booth — brother of Lincoln's assassin John Wilkes Booth — purchased the theatre in 1863. 

So, seeing 1776 there — a play about the founding of America, set in Philadelphia, performed in a building that's been standing since 1808 — is about as historically layered an experience as live theater gets.

The Story

1776 depicts historical events from May 8 through July 4, 1776, with a sprinkling of dramatic license. It begins on a sweltering day in Philadelphia with the Second Continental Congress in session. John Adams, the Massachusetts representative, is enumerating his grievances against King George III and lobbying for independence. The other delegates, already divisive and annoyed by his arguments, demand in the song "Sit Down, John" that he be quiet. 

Adams has also been long separated from his wife, Abigail — their letters and his imagination bring them briefly together, with him demanding that the women of Massachusetts send saltpeter for gunpowder, and her demanding that Congress send pins for sewing. 

The central challenge is getting enough votes. Adams enlists Franklin and eventually Thomas Jefferson — reluctant to write anything because he misses his wife Martha — to draft the Declaration. The biggest obstacle is the slavery question: Southern delegates led by Edward Rutledge threaten to walk out unless all language condemning slavery is struck from the document, a painful compromise the independence faction ultimately accepts.
After more debate, the final vote is cast by James Wilson, who votes in favor not so much from personal conviction, but because he does not want to be remembered as "the man who prevented American independence." The play closes as the delegates gather one by one to sign the Declaration, with the Liberty Bell tolling as the curtain falls. 

Historical Context

The musical was a passion project by Sherman Edwards, a history teacher who also composed on the side. He left his jobs and spent 9 years researching and writing it. His goal was to show the Founding Fathers "at their outermost limits — men who disagreed and fought with each other." 

Produced on the eve of the nation's bicentennial, in the charged political climate of the 1960s and '70s, 1776 showed how the nation began in conflict. It was sometimes seen as a conservative answer to the hippie movement of the late 1960s, which had spawned Hair. 

It premiered on Broadway in 1969 to warm reviews, ran for 1,217 performances, was nominated for five Tony Awards and won three, including Best Musical. 

Major Productions Over the Years

1969 Original Broadway — William Daniels starred as John Adams, with Howard Da Silva as Benjamin Franklin — Da Silva had a heart attack after the final preview but insisted on performing opening night. The show became a landmark of American musical theater. 

1972 Film — The musical was made into a film of the same name, with much of the original cast. It's considered one of the more faithful Broadway-to-film adaptations. 

1997 Broadway Revival — Directed by Scott Ellis and choreographed by Kathleen Marshall, it starred Brent Spiner as Adams, Gregg Edelman, Pat Hingle, and Tom Aldredge. It ran through June 1998. 

2016 Encores! at City Center — This concert production embraced diversity with John Larroquette as Franklin, Santino Fontana as Adams, AndrÃ© De Shields as Stephen Hopkins, and Jubilant Sykes as Richard Henry Lee. 

2022 Broadway Revival — The boldest reinvention yet. A multiracial cast of females, transgender, and nonbinary actors portrayed the fiery founders, putting history in the hands of the humans who were left out the first time around. Crystal Lucas-Perry played Adams, Patrena Murray played Franklin, Elizabeth A. Davis played Jefferson, and Carolee Carmello played John Dickinson. The production was co-directed by Diane Paulus — known for Waitress — and Jeffrey L. Page. Critics called it "very funny, with a jaunty and tuneful score — a win for life and liberty." 

Why It Still Resonates

1776 is considered a trailblazer for contemporary history musicals — Hamilton even includes the lyric "sit down, John" as a direct nod, and both shows share Thomas Jefferson as a character and use non-traditional casting to reflect modern America. The Walnut Street Theatre, being right in Philadelphia where these events actually took place, is one of the most fitting stages imaginable for it — and as one of America's oldest theaters, it carries its own bit of revolutionary-era history. 

#walnutstreettheatre #philadelphia #250America
